question: Do people with the exposure go on to get the outcome more often?

vandenbroucke2007.cite: Vandenbroucke et al. (2007). Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE): explanation and elaboration. PLoS Medicine 4(10): e297.
vandenbroucke2007.checked: every quote read word for word in the Europe PMC full text (PMC2020496) on 20 Nov 2026; the article is online-only (e297), so places are given as its STROBE items and boxes; in-text reference numbers are left out of the quotes

steps.title: Recruit
steps.text: Define who is eligible and enrol a group that is free of the outcome at the start.

quotes.text: Closed cohorts (for example birth cohorts) enrol a defined number of participants at study onset and follow them from that time forward, often at set intervals up to a fixed end date.

steps.title: Measure exposure
steps.text: Record each person's exposure at the start, before any outcome has happened, so the time order is clear.

quotes.text: They obtain information about people and their exposures at baseline, let time pass, and then assess the occurrence of outcomes.

steps.title: Follow up
steps.text: Follow everyone the same way for years, and keep track of who is lost along the way.

quotes.text: Knowing details about follow-up procedures, including whether procedures minimized non-response and loss to follow-up and whether the procedures were similar for all participants, informs judgments about the validity of results.

steps.title: Count new cases
steps.text: Count the people who develop the outcome during follow-up, in each exposure group.

quotes.text: They may examine the number of people who have a disease at a particular time (prevalence), or that develop a disease over a defined period (incidence).

steps.title: Compare risks
steps.text: Divide the risk (or rate) in the exposed by that in the unexposed. Adjust for confounders, because exposure was not assigned by chance.

quotes.text: In a closed cohort cumulative incidences (risks) and incidence rates can be estimated; when exposed and unexposed groups are compared, this leads to risk ratio or rate ratio estimates.

confounding.text: In reality, the seeming association or lack of association is due to another factor that determines the occurrence of the disease but that is also associated with the exposure.

attrition.text: In other studies where follow-up procedures differed between exposed and unexposed groups, readers might recognize substantial bias due to unequal ascertainment of events or differences in non-response or loss to follow-up

limits: The Framingham Study's own design (Dawber et al. 1951, the card's reference) was not read in this task; the steps follow the STROBE explanation instead.
STROBE itself avoids the words prospective and retrospective (item 4); this page uses prospective for a cohort whose exposure is measured before the outcomes occur.
The picture's numbers (3 of 9 against 1 of 9) are made up to show the arithmetic.
